title: Why Your Time-Out Must Be Longer
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that a broader culture of leniency in schools has stripped away real accountability, making classroom management more essential than ever, and that time-out is one lever nearly every teacher can strengthen. He lists prerequisites for effective time-out, including students knowing the rules cold, understanding the 'why,' having every step modeled, and consistent enforcement without added lecturing. He pairs this with the teacher's own obligation to make the regular classroom genuinely engaging through expert instruction, energy, humor, and shifted responsibility, so that time-out actually feels like a loss. His central claim is that in today's low-accountability climate, common advice to keep time-out brief (tied to a student's age) is outdated; he recommends 12-15 minutes for primary students and 15-20-plus minutes for older students, listing specific psychological needs — calming down, feeling the weight of accountability, resolving not to repeat the mistake — that only a longer duration reliably meets. He concludes that longer time-outs paradoxically produce less total time in time-out over a school year.
points: A broader culture of leniency in schools has removed real accountability, making strong classroom management essential.
Effective time-out requires students to know the rules, understand the why, see it modeled, and face 100% consistent enforcement without lecturing.
Teachers must also make the regular classroom genuinely engaging so that time-out feels like a real loss by contrast.
He recommends 12-15 minutes for primary-age students and 15-20-plus minutes for older students, longer than commonly advised.
Longer time-outs let students calm down, feel real accountability, and resolve not to repeat the mistake, ultimately reducing total time spent in time-out over the year.
quotes: A culture of leniency has infected our schools from top to bottom, and it’s hurting everyone in its wake.
One area through which almost every teacher can improve behavior is time-out.
But in a climate of little to no accountability your students need to feel time-out. Not as an extended punishment, but as a time to reflect on their mistake and how it affects others.
12 to 15 minutes isn’t too long for for primary age students. Yes, even kindergartners. And 15 or 20 minutes or more for older students.
Over the course of a school year, not only will longer time-outs result in better and more respectful behavior, but they’ll result in far less total time in time-out.
